power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .256", "p = 0.4790", "p = 0.085" ), Sentence = c("A likelihood-ratio test against the unadjusted model is non-significant (LRT = 2.73, df = 2, p = .256), indicating no detectable selection bias, and the model-adjusted estimate (r = .133, 95% CI [.045, .218]) remains positive and significant", "The results indicated that while mean age was not a significant moderator (b = 0.0012, p = 0.4790), age range significantly predicted the magnitude of the correlation (b = 0.0041, p = 0.0038), suggesting that studies with a wider age range reported stronger positive correlations.", "Mean age was non-significant in every specification (smallest p = 0.085)." )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: Psychological acceptance is an emotion regulation strategy in which people allow thoughts and feelings to arise and pass without trying to change them.
Although theory implies that acceptance will increase with age, empirical evidence remains fragmented, with studies varying in sample characteristics, effect sizes, and age ranges.
To address this gap and clarify the association between age and psychological acceptance we conducted a meta-analysis.
Our preregistered search (PROSPERO CRD420251103979) identified 25 studies with 31 independent samples (N = 12,561).
Random-effects pooling yielded a small but robust positive association between age and psychological acceptance (r = 0.077, 95% CI 0.027-0.127), despite substantial heterogeneity between studies.
Specifically, studies that sampled wider age ranges reported stronger associations, so narrow age spans may understate the association.
People regulate their emotions to influence what they feel, when they feel it, and how they express it (Gross, 1998 (Gross, , 2015)).
text.formatted: People regulate their emotions to influence what they feel, when they feel it, and how they express it <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Gross, 1998</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Gross, , 2015))</ref>.

text.text: They do so through distinct strategies.
Each strategy acts at a different point in the emotion-generative process and carries different consequences for affect, physiology and wellbeing (Gross, 2015).
text.formatted: Each strategy acts at a different point in the emotion-generative process and carries different consequences for affect, physiology and wellbeing <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Gross, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Cognitive reappraisal, for example, involves deliberately generating an alternative interpretation of a stressful situation to reduce its emotional impact (Gross, 1998).
text.formatted: Cognitive reappraisal, for example, involves deliberately generating an alternative interpretation of a stressful situation to reduce its emotional impact <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Gross, 1998)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, psychological acceptance is a receptive, noninterfering stance toward momentary experience.
Rather than suppress, avoid, alter or prolong an experience, acceptance lets it arise, unfold and pass naturally, regardless of valence (Lindsay & Creswell, 2019; Wolfe & Isaacowitz, 2022).
text.formatted: Rather than suppress, avoid, alter or prolong an experience, acceptance lets it arise, unfold and pass naturally, regardless of valence <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Lindsay & Creswell, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Wolfe & Isaacowitz, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: It changes how individuals relate to their thoughts and feelings, not the content of those experiences, so they may regulate their emotions without modifying them (Dunn et al., 2009; Troy et al., 2018).
text.formatted: It changes how individuals relate to their thoughts and feelings, not the content of those experiences, so they may regulate their emotions without modifying them <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Dunn et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Troy et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Because acceptance involves no attempt to modify an experience, it may demand less cognitive effort than strategies that do (Gross, 1998; Lindsay & Creswell, 2019; Wolfe & Isaacowitz, 2022).
text.formatted: Because acceptance involves no attempt to modify an experience, it may demand less cognitive effort than strategies that do <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Gross, 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Lindsay & Creswell, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Wolfe & Isaacowitz, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Acceptance is also associated with a range of positive outcomes. Thompson et al. (2011) reviewed mostly correlational studies using self-report measures of psychological acceptance.
text.formatted: Acceptance is also associated with a range of positive outcomes. <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Thompson et al. (2011)</ref> reviewed mostly correlational studies using self-report measures of psychological acceptance.

text.text: They found that higher acceptance went together with lower post-traumatic distress across diverse samples (Cavanagh et al., 2014; Thompson et al., 2011).
text.formatted: They found that higher acceptance went together with lower post-traumatic distress across diverse samples <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Cavanagh et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Thompson et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Psychological acceptance has also been linked to improved adaptation to health-related stressors.
For example, among breast cancer patients, acceptance was associated with lower levels of psychological distress in a crosssectional study (N = 79) (Politi et al., 2007).
text.formatted: For example, among breast cancer patients, acceptance was associated with lower levels of psychological distress in a crosssectional study (N = 79) <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Politi et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, in a short-term, prospective, multi-method design, Shallcross et al. (2013) provided empirical evidence linking acceptance in everyday contexts with reduced negative affect, highlighting its role as a psychological process that may support emotional well-being (Shallcross et al., 2013).

(2013)</ref> provided empirical evidence linking acceptance in everyday contexts with reduced negative affect, highlighting its role as a psychological process that may support emotional well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Shallcross et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Psychological acceptance may increase with age (Shallcross et al., 2013) and peak in older adulthood (Schirda et al., 2016; Wolfe & Isaacowitz, 2022).
text.formatted: Psychological acceptance may increase with age <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Shallcross et al., 2013)</ref> and peak in older adulthood <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Schirda et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Wolfe & Isaacowitz, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Three explanations may account for this trend.
First, as cognitive processing resources decline with age, older adults may favor emotion regulation strategies that place fewer demands on cognitive resources (Urry & Gross, 2010).
text.formatted: First, as cognitive processing resources decline with age, older adults may favor emotion regulation strategies that place fewer demands on cognitive resources <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Urry & Gross, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Psychological acceptance is easier to implement than other emotion regulation strategies (Alberts et al., 2012; Troy et al., 2018).

text.text: It may therefore require fewer cognitive resources and suit older adults (Shallcross et al., 2013; Wolfe & Isaacowitz, 2022).
text.formatted: It may therefore require fewer cognitive resources and suit older adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Shallcross et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Wolfe & Isaacowitz, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Second, older adulthood often brings fundamental and irreversible losses, such as the death of loved ones and physical decline (Kunzmann & Grühn, 2005; Lang, 2001).
text.formatted: Second, older adulthood often brings fundamental and irreversible losses, such as the death of loved ones and physical decline <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Kunzmann & Grühn, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Lang, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Because people cannot reverse these losses, acceptance may serve them better than strategies that aim to change the situation (Shallcross et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Because people cannot reverse these losses, acceptance may serve them better than strategies that aim to change the situation <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Shallcross et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Losses also tend to elicit sadness, and people use acceptance more often in response to experimentally induced sadness than fear (Vishkin et al., 2020; Wolfe & Isaacowitz, 2022).

text.text: Older adults face such losses more often and may therefore rely on acceptance more.
Third, older adults show a clear preference for positive affect (such as joy, contentment and interest), particularly low-arousal positive affect (Riediger et al., 2009; Scheibe et al., 2013).

text.text: Psychological acceptance reduces negative affect (Kober et al., 2019a) and physiological reactivity to affective stimuli (Low et al., 2008; Troy et al., 2018).

text.text: It therefore offers older adults a route to calmer, low arousal states (Riediger et al., 2009; Wolfe & Isaacowitz, 2022).
text.formatted: It therefore offers older adults a route to calmer, low arousal states <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Riediger et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Wolfe & Isaacowitz, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: These accounts are consistent with evidence pointing to the benefits of psychological acceptance in older adulthood.

In a study of adults aged 64 to 83, participants reported greater motivation to use psychological acceptance, and greater success in using it compared to either detachment or positive reappraisal strategies (Rompilla et al., 2022).
text.formatted: In a study of adults aged 64 to 83, participants reported greater motivation to use psychological acceptance, and greater success in using it compared to either detachment or positive reappraisal strategies <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Rompilla et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Qualitative accounts converge with the pattern.
Older adults living alone with chronic illness describe acceptance of their circumstances as central to coping with declining health (Birkeland & Natvig, 2009).

text.text: Similarly, among community-dwelling and care-receiving older adults aged 65 to 96, higher psychological acceptance, was associated with better subjective and objective quality of life across multiple domains (Butler & Ciarrochi, 2007).

text.text: Published age-acceptance correlations differ in size and direction, and about a third of the samples we identified include fewer than 200 participants.
However, single studies are often underpowered to establish the reliability and size of an effect.
Furthermore, in a relatively small body of literature, a few influential studies or selective publication can inflate an apparent effect.
Finally, studies reporting the age-acceptance associations were rarely designed to examine agerelated change, and they differ markedly in mean age and in the range of age represented.
Thus, sample composition may itself account for part of the variation observed across samples and measures.
The present meta-analysis therefore pursues three aims that address the gaps identified above.
First, it estimates the pooled association between age and psychological acceptance across adulthood.
Second, it tests the robustness of this estimate against outliers, influential cases and publication bias.
Third, it examines whether mean age and age range moderate the magnitude of the association.
The moderator analysis offers an initial, if indirect, indication of whether age differences extend across adulthood or emerge only in later life.
Beyond its scientific contribution, the study may carry practical implications.
Previous studies linked psychological acceptance to better well-being (Butler & Ciarrochi, 2007; Kober et al., 2019b; Shallcross et al., 2013).

text.text: If psychological acceptance rises with age, interventions for older adults that build psychological acceptance may be better aligned with their existing emotion regulation tendencies and strengths.
We conducted a systematic literature search following the PRISMA guidelines to identify studies examining the association between age and psychological acceptance across the adult lifespan.
The search was performed on 25 November 2025 across three major bibliographic databases: PsycInfo, PubMed, and Scopus.
Our search strategy relied on three conceptual pillars: age-related terms, psychological acceptance as a construct, and validated psychometric instruments.
We registered the protocol at PROSPERO (CRD420251103979).
To ensure comprehensive coverage, we utilized both controlled vocabulary (where available) and free-text terms in article titles, abstracts, and keywords.

The targeted instruments included the Acceptance and Action Questionnaire (AAQ/AAQ-II) (Hayes, 2004)  (Bond et al., 2011), the Emotion Acceptance Questionnaire (EAQ) (Kisley et al., 2025), the Kentucky Inventory of Mindfulness Skills (KIMS) (Baer et al., 2004), the Philadelphia Mindfulness Scale (PHLMS) (Cardaciotto et al., 2008), the Cognitive Emotion Regulation Questionnaire (CERQ) (Garnefski et al., 2001), the COPE questionnaire (Carver, 1989), the Emotion Regulation Strategy Scale (ERSS) (Kneeland et al., 2024) and the Impermanence Awareness and Acceptance Scale (IMAAS) (Fernández-Campos et al., 2021).
text.formatted: The targeted instruments included the Acceptance and Action Questionnaire (AAQ/AAQ-II) <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Hayes, 2004)</ref>  <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bond et al., 2011)</ref>, the Emotion Acceptance Questionnaire (EAQ) <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Kisley et al., 2025)</ref>, the Kentucky Inventory of Mindfulness Skills (KIMS) <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Baer et al., 2004)</ref>, the Philadelphia Mindfulness Scale (PHLMS) <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Cardaciotto et al., 2008)</ref>, the Cognitive Emotion Regulation Questionnaire (CERQ) <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Garnefski et al., 2001)</ref>, the COPE questionnaire <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Carver, 1989)</ref>, the Emotion Regulation Strategy Scale (ERSS) <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Kneeland et al., 2024)</ref> and the Impermanence Awareness and Acceptance Scale (IMAAS) <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Fernández-Campos et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: To capture broader nomenclature, the terms "Acceptance Questionnaire" and "Acceptance Scale" were also included.
The search yielded a total of 234 records.
Following the removal of 51 duplicate records, 183 unique records remained and were screened at the title and abstract level.
Of these, 90 records were excluded because they did not meet initial eligibility criteria.
The remaining 93 full-text reports were retrieved and assessed for eligibility.

Of these, 1 report was not retrieved and 71 reports were excluded: 69 because they lacked sufficient statistical information, even after attempts to obtain the missing data from the authors, one because the age of the participants was under 18 and one because it was not published in English.
Ultimately, 21 studies met all inclusion criteria and were therefore included in the metaanalysis.
All records identified through database searches were independently screened by two reviewers at both the title and abstract level, followed by full-text review.
Inter-reviewer agreement was high, and any disagreements regarding eligibility or data extraction were resolved through discussion.
Instances where consensus could not be reached were resolved by a third reviewer acting as an arbiter.
To capture relevant studies that the database search might have missed, we also screened the reference lists of included studies.
This process yielded 44 potentially relevant citations.

Of these, 5 were excluded during the initial abstract-based screening, and 35 were excluded at the full-text stage due to insufficient reported data that we were not able to complete by contacting the authors.
For the remaining 4 papers identified as potentially eligible, the second reviewer independently assessed and verified their full texts to confirm their final inclusion.
Consequently, 4 additional studies were included.
As a result, the final meta-analysis comprised 25 studies.
Notably, two of these studies provided data from multiple independent samples.
In these instances, effect sizes were calculated separately for each sample.

text.text: The database search of PsycInfo, PubMed, and Scopus returned 234 records.
After 51 duplicates were removed, 183 records were screened at the title and abstract level, of which 90 were excluded for not meeting the initial eligibility criteria.

The remaining 93 full-text reports were assessed for eligibility; one report could not be retrieved, and 71 were excluded, primarily for insufficient statistical information after author contact (n = 69), lack of English-language publication (n = 1) or samples of individuals under 18 (n = 1), leaving 21 studies.

In addition, citation searching via other methods identified 44 records; 39 reports were sought for retrieval and assessed for eligibility, of which 35 were excluded for insufficient statistical information, leaving 4 additional studies included, for a total of 25 included studies.
Studies were eligible for inclusion if they reported empirical correlation coefficients (Pearson's r) or provided sufficient statistical data to calculate an effect size.
For potentially eligible studies lacking essential data, we contacted the authors.

We excluded studies that: (a) utilized non-quantitative designs or lacked primary data; (b) conceptualized psychological acceptance as a non-psychological construct (e.g., technology acceptance); (c) utilized populationspecific or context-dependent adaptations of psychological acceptance measures rather than general validated scales; (d) focused on samples under 18 years of age; (e) did not treat age as an independent variable; or (f) were not published in English.
Data extraction was performed using a standardized form.

The extracted variables included study identifiers and sample characteristics (authors and year, sample size, age range, mean age, and age SD), psychometric measures (scale name), and statistical indices necessary for effect size calculation (Pearson's r, Cohen's d, η², t values, regression coefficients B and β, confidence intervals, and p values).
A formal risk of bias assessment tool was not utilized, as the scope of this correlational meta-analysis focused primarily on bivariate associations across heterogeneous observational designs.
The primary effect size metric used in the analysis was Pearson's correlation coefficient (r).
Where r was not reported directly, it was calculated from alternative statistical indices using algebraic transformation formulas.
Specifically, for Enoki et al. (2018), the psychological acceptance score comprised two subscales, and we averaged their correlations with age (r = .11 and r = .17) into a single effect size.

text.text: Because transformations from squared indices discard directional information, the sign of the converted effect size was manually recovered and assigned by cross-referencing the direction of the descriptive statistics and textual reporting in the original paper.

To ensure a consistent interpretation of the pooled estimates, correlation coefficients from instruments measuring constructs opposite to psychological acceptance had their signs reversed, establishing a convention where a positive value consistently indicates greater psychological acceptance at older ages.

The reversed measures included the AAQ (9-item) (Hayes, 2004), AAQ-II (Bond et al., 2011) and CFQ-7 (Cognitive Fusion Questionnaire) (Gillanders et al., 2014) In the reported study, AAQ-II and CFQ-7 total scores were summed to produce a total psychological inflexibility score, which was used in the present analysis.

The sampling variance (𝑣) for each study was calculated as 𝑣 = 1 𝑁-3 .
All final results were back transformed to Pearson's r for interpretative clarity.

In addition, a 95% prediction interval was calculated to estimate the expected range of true effects in future comparable studies.

text.text: To evaluate the robustness of our results, we performed diagnostic analyses.
We conducted a leave-one-out sensitivity analysis and influence diagnostics to identify any studies exerting disproportionate leverage on the model.
We then assessed potential publication bias using a funnel plot and Egger's regression test.
To address the asymmetry identified by these tests, we applied the 'Trim and Fill' method.

However, because both Egger's test and the Trim and Fill method can perform poorly under conditions of substantial between-study heterogeneity, we additionally implemented a selection model as a complementary check.
To explore potential moderators of the relationship between age and psychological acceptance, we performed a meta-regression analysis using a Restricted Maximum Likelihood (REML) estimator.

Because previous studies were rarely designed to examine age-related differences and varied substantially in their sample age distributions, we included the mean age and the age range of the sample as continuous predictors to assess whether variations in these demographic characteristics accounted for significant heterogeneity in the observed effects.
Age range was calculated as the difference between the maximum and minimum age reported within each sample.

Of the 31 studies included in the overall meta-analysis, 23 provided sufficient information and were retained in this specific analysis, whereas 8 studies were excluded due to missing demographic details.
Prior to the analysis, potential multicollinearity between the two predictors was evaluated.
To evaluate the robustness of the meta-regression, we re-estimated the model 23 times, omitting one sample each time.
We recorded the coefficients and 95% confidence intervals for mean age and age range from each refit.
We also inspected studentized residuals, Cook's distances and hat values (Viechtbauer et al., 2015).

text.text: Studentized residuals flag samples whose effect size lies far from the model prediction.
Cook's distances flag samples whose removal shifts the coefficients.
Hat values measure leverage, meaning how far a sample's mean age and age range lie from those of the other samples.
A sample with high leverage can pull the fitted regression line towards itself.
We therefore repeated the test of the moderators in two ways.
The Knapp-Hartung adjustment modifies the standard errors of the coefficients (Knapp & Hartung, 2003).

text.text: We then re-estimated the model three more times to check that specific analytic choices did not drive the result.
First, we excluded the effect sizes derived from other test statistics, because they come from conversion formulas rather than reported correlations.
Second, we excluded the sample recruited in two disjoint age bands (18 to 29 and 60 to 86 years).
Its age range of 68 years describes a sample with no participants aged 30 to 59 years.
The range therefore does not reflect a continuous distribution of ages.
Third, we excluded papers that contributed more than one sample, because samples from the same paper share methods and measures and may yield correlated effects.

Across 25 studies and 31 independent samples (N = 12,561), age correlated positively with psychological acceptance.
The association was small (r = .077, 95% CI [.027, .127]) and robust to influence and publication-bias analyses.
It also varied widely between studies (95% prediction interval -.17 to .32).
Samples with wider age ranges showed stronger associations (b = .0041), whereas mean age did not moderate the association.
The findings offer the first meta-analytic test of the lifespan prediction that psychological acceptance rises with age.
They also show that the age span sampled in a study shapes the association it will detect, so studies of narrow age bands may underestimate the association between psychological acceptance and age.
The positive association aligns closely with foundational lifespan frameworks.

Socioemotional selectivity theory (Carstensen, 1993; Carstensen et al., 1999) proposes that perceiving one's remaining time as limited shifts priorities toward emotionally meaningful experiences and close social relationships.

text.text: Psychological acceptance may support these priorities by helping people respond to circumstances they cannot change without becoming caught in a struggle against them.
Psychological acceptance may be particularly relevant in later life, when coping with uncontrollable and irreversible losses (Kunzmann & Grühn, 2005; Lang, 2001; Shallcross et al., 2013).

text.text: A complementary perspective attributes the increase in acceptance to growing wisdom (Ardelt, 2000) that is characterized by the ability to recognize and manage the uncertainty inherent in human life (Baltes & Smith, 2008).
text.formatted: A complementary perspective attributes the increase in acceptance to growing wisdom <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Ardelt, 2000)</ref> that is characterized by the ability to recognize and manage the uncertainty inherent in human life <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Baltes & Smith, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: From this perspective, psychological acceptance may reflect a growing capacity to integrate uncertainty and impermanence into one's understanding of life.
The wisdom account offers a possible developmental explanation for greater psychological acceptance with age, although wisdom should not be assumed to increase uniformly across individuals.
Sample age range, rather than mean age, moderated the association.
Studies reporting ageacceptance associations were rarely designed to examine broad age-related change.
Instead, many studies focus on relatively narrow age ranges.

The age-range effect is consistent with, though does not establish, a lifespan account in which psychological acceptance increases across adulthood, as wider age spans allow developmental differences to emerge more clearly.

However, the same pattern may also reflect a statistical range-restriction effect, whereby studies including narrower age ranges have reduced ability to detect age-acceptance associations due to limited variability in age.
Because the present analyses were based on cross-sectional associations, they cannot distinguish between these explanations.

Longitudinal research will therefore be required to determine whether psychological acceptance increases continuously across adulthood or whether changes are concentrated during specific developmental transitions.
Age range explained part of the variability between studies, but substantial residual heterogeneity remained.

The included literature differed in ways we could not test, including samples composed exclusively of a single gender, specific occupational groups (e.g., psychiatrists), or clinical cohorts (e.g., individuals with acquired brain injury).
We did not evaluate these sources of variation because they were not specified as a priori moderation hypotheses and statistical power for subgroup comparisons was limited.
Residual heterogeneity may also reflect age-related challenges that constrain the use of psychological acceptance under certain conditions.
Physiological changes can leave older adults less equipped to recover from sustained emotional arousal (Charles, 2010).
text.formatted: Physiological changes can leave older adults less equipped to recover from sustained emotional arousal <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Charles, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Perceived and actual proximity to death may pose additional challenges, as losses and declines near the end of life can overwhelm otherwise effective emotion regulation (Palgi et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Perceived and actual proximity to death may pose additional challenges, as losses and declines near the end of life can overwhelm otherwise effective emotion regulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Palgi et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: In line with this, research indicates that psychological acceptance is more frequently deployed in response to low-intensity rather than high-intensity negative emotions (Lennarz et al., 2019).
text.formatted: In line with this, research indicates that psychological acceptance is more frequently deployed in response to low-intensity rather than high-intensity negative emotions <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Lennarz et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Future primary studies could measure emotional intensity and proximity to death alongside psychological acceptance.
Several limitations warrant consideration.
First, the data are predominantly cross-sectional, so they cannot detect age trajectories in psychological acceptance.
Second, the substantial between-study heterogeneity and the prediction interval indicate that significant residual variance remains unexplained by sample age range alone.
The pooled estimate therefore represents a broad central tendency rather than an identical developmental trajectory shared by all individuals.
Measurement also constrains the findings.

Our search strategy identified five distinct types of questionnaires (AAQ, CERQ, COPE, PHLMS, and COF), several of which included multiple adaptations, such as short forms, older and updated versions, or translations.

Despite this breadth, the published evidence base was dominated by studies using the Acceptance and Action Questionnaire, with 22 out of the 31 extracted effect sizes belonging to the AAQ family (and particularly the AAQ-II).
Consequently, current empirical knowledge remains disproportionately weighted toward findings derived from this specific measure.
Furthermore, the literature mainly relies on self-report methodologies.

Although inclusion was restricted to psychometrically validated instruments, self-reports remain vulnerable to age-related shifts in item interpretation, response styles, or social desirability biases.
A further limitation concerns the studies that could not be included.
Of the 95 full-text reports assessed for eligibility, 73 were excluded because they did not report sufficient statistical information despite attempts to contact the authors.
Age was rarely a focal variable in these reports, so whether an age-acceptance correlation was reported at all may depend on what that correlation showed.
The present synthesis therefore rests on a subset of studies that reported the association, and the direction of any resulting bias cannot be determined from the available data.
Finally, the funnel plot warrants comment.
Egger's test indicated asymmetry, but its direction ran counter to selective suppression: smaller studies reported smaller associations, not larger ones.
A selection model found no evidence of selection, so the analyses gave no indication that the pooled estimate is inflated by reporting bias.
The asymmetry reflects a small-study effect.
The present moderators explain only part of the heterogeneity, so the source of this effect remains unclear.
To address these limitations, future research should prioritize longitudinal designs capable of capturing intra-individual trajectories of psychological acceptance across adulthood.
Such studies should employ measurement instruments explicitly validated for psychometric equivalence across diverse age cohorts alongside behavioral indices of psychological acceptance.
Future primary studies should also record participant demographics so that potential moderators of the residual heterogeneity can be tested.
Across 31 independent effect sizes, we observed a small but reliable positive association, indicating that psychological acceptance tends to be higher at older ages.
Meta-regression showed that studies employing wider sample age ranges yielded significantly larger effect sizes, indicating that narrow age ranges may understate the association across adulthood.

Whether psychological acceptance develops gradually across adulthood or emerges mainly in later life is yet to be examined, and wide age range longitudinal designs are needed to address this question. and validity analysis in clinical and non-clinical samples.
